teaser: A queen is leaving, but the real star of this harbor is the sun.
review_notes:
Size about 149 x 194 cm (59 x 76 in).
Painted for Frédéric-Maurice de La Tour d'Auvergne, Duc de Bouillon, general of the papal army, as a pair with 'Landscape with the Marriage of Isaac and Rebecca' (The Mill), both in the National Gallery.
Both came with the Angerstein collection, bought by the British government in 1824 to found the National Gallery.
Turner's bequest condition (his 'Dido building Carthage' and 'Sun rising through Vapour' to hang between the two Claudes): well documented.
The pastry-cook story comes from early biographer Joachim von Sandrart and is doubted by some scholars; told as 'an early biographer says'.
Liber Veritatis: about 195 drawings, now in the British Museum.
Identification of the queen as the figure in a pink-red dress and crown coming down the steps at about (0.84, 0.66) was made on a small image; please check the spot on a high-resolution file.
The sun is described as rising (morning departure), the usual reading.

lesson.text: If you had to paint a queen setting off on the most famous journey of her life, where would you put her? In the middle, surely, and large. Claude Lorrain did neither. In this picture the Queen of Sheba is a figure smaller than your fingernail, and you may need a minute to find her.

The story comes from the Bible. The Queen of Sheba, ruler of a rich kingdom far to the south, hears of the wisdom of King Solomon and travels to Jerusalem to test him with hard questions. The Bible speaks of her arrival with camels and gold. It says nothing about a harbor.

So Claude invented the scene. He imagined the morning she leaves home: a palace by the water, a small boat waiting at the quay, and a ship anchored farther out. Almost no painter had shown this moment before him.
The queen is coming down from her palace toward the water, with her attendants around her. Tap her.

spots.title: The queen
spots.text: There, on the palace steps, in a pink-red dress with a small gold crown, in the middle of a cluster of attendants. She is one figure in a crowd, on her way down to the boat.

lesson.text: Why make the heroine so small? Because Claude was a landscape painter, and in Rome in the 1640s landscape ranked low. Serious art was supposed to tell great stories. A biblical title let him sell to grand clients what he truly wanted to paint: air, water and light.

An early biographer says Claude arrived in Italy as a teenage pastry cook and entered a painter's household as a servant before becoming a pupil. Born in the duchy of Lorraine around 1600, he signed his French name Gellée, but all Europe called him simply Claude.

The boldest decision is in the center. Painters before him usually kept the sun out of the frame and showed only its effects. Claude turns you to face it. The sun sits low over the sea, and every other thing in the picture is organized around that glow.
Three lines show how the picture leads you to the light.

lines.label: The horizon
lines.text: The sea meets the sky a little below the middle of the canvas. The sun hangs just above this line, so close that its glow dissolves the far shore.

lines.label: The path on the water
lines.text: Under the sun, a column of bright ripples runs down toward you. The waves get larger and darker as they come closer: that is how Claude measures distance.

lines.label: The palace roofline
lines.text: The long cornice of the palace slopes down and inward. Follow it past the round tower and your eye is delivered to the bright center of the sky.

lesson.text: Notice what stands at the sides: a ruined colonnade on the left, the palace on the right, both dark against the sky. Claude borrowed the idea from the theater, where painted flats frame the stage. The two wings make the glowing gap between them feel deeper.
Claude made light itself the subject. Buildings, ships and people are arranged like stage scenery so that your eye travels, step by step, into the sun.

He prepared for this outdoors. Friends described him walking out of Rome before dawn to watch the sky change and sketching in the countryside. Back in the studio he rebuilt those observations into ideal places that never existed, more harmonious than any real port.

Claude's pictures were so sought after that forgers copied his style while he was alive. His defense was a book: he drew a record of each painting he sold, with the buyer's name on the back. He called it the Liber Veritatis, Latin for “book of truth.”

This canvas, about 1.5 meters high and almost 2 meters wide (59 by 76 inches), was ordered in 1648 by a French duke who commanded the pope's army. With so much room, Claude filled the harbor with small scenes of work. They are worth a slow walk.

spots.title: Loading the luggage
spots.text: In the foreground, men haul a heavy red-patterned trunk into a rowboat. This is the busiest, most physical spot in the picture, placed where the queen should have been.

spots.title: The waiting boat
spots.text: A long decorated boat with rowers is tied up at the foot of the steps. It will carry the queen out to the ship anchored in the bay.

spots.title: The ship
spots.text: Her vessel waits at anchor, a dark outline against the brightest part of the sea. Its masts and flags are drawn with a fine brush, almost like pen lines.

spots.title: Shading his eyes
spots.text: A figure lounging on the quay lifts an arm to his head against the glare. He does what you would do. Claude uses him to make you feel the brightness.

spots.title: The ruined column
spots.text: A fluted column with a leafy capital, plants growing on the broken stone above. The style is Roman, and already old and crumbling in a story set centuries before Rome.

spots.title: Sailors in the rigging
spots.text: Behind the columns a big ship is getting ready. Tiny sailors climb the mast and work the sail: the harbor is waking up.

spots.title: Two onlookers
spots.text: Two men stand with their backs half turned, one in a red cloak, chatting as they watch. Figures seen from behind invite you to stand next to them and look.

spots.title: The palace
spots.text: A fantasy building with statues on the roof and spectators on the balcony. Its style is that of the grand villas Claude saw being built around Rome.

lesson.text: English collectors fell in love with Claude. In the 1700s they bought his paintings by the dozen, and landowners reshaped their parks with lakes, temples and clumps of trees so that the view from the house would look like one of his pictures.

In 1824 the British government bought a banker's collection of 38 paintings to start a national museum. This harbor was among them. It has belonged to the National Gallery in London since the very first day.

The English painter J. M. W. Turner was obsessed with this picture. When he left his own works to the nation, he set a condition: two of them had to hang beside this Claude and its companion. They still do, in the same room of the National Gallery.

quiz.question: Where is the Queen of Sheba in the painting?
options: On the deck of the big ship
Small, on the palace steps at the right
quiz.explanation: She comes down the steps among her attendants, a tiny figure in a crowd.

quiz.question: What was unusual about the way Claude treated the sun?
options: He placed it in the picture, facing the viewer
quiz.explanation: Earlier painters mostly showed only the sun's effects, not the sun itself.

quiz.question: What was the Liber Veritatis?
options: A prayer book owned by the queen
Claude's drawn record of his paintings, to fight forgeries
quiz.explanation: He drew each painting he sold in this “book of truth.”

quiz.question: Which part of the story did Claude have to invent?
quiz.explanation: The Bible describes her visit but never mentions a seaport.

quiz.question: What did Turner demand in his will?
options: That two of his paintings hang beside this Claude and its pair
That the Claude be sent back to Rome
That his paintings never be shown with older art
quiz.explanation: His two canvases still hang next to the Claudes in London.

quiz.question: What role do the colonnade and the palace play?
options: They frame the bright center like stage wings
They show where the queen lives and sleeps
quiz.explanation: Dark shapes at both sides make the glowing middle feel deeper.

facts.text: The painting entered the National Gallery in the 1900s.
facts.explanation: It was part of the founding purchase of 1824.

facts.text: In Claude's time, landscape was considered a lower kind of painting than scenes from history or the Bible.
facts.explanation: That is why he attached a biblical story to his harbor view.

facts.text: The harbor shows a real port that Claude copied on the spot.
facts.explanation: It is an ideal place he composed in the studio from his outdoor observations.
